name: Synopsys
subcategory: Full-flow EDA, silicon IP and simulation
role: Supplies the synthesis, place-and-route, verification and signoff software used to turn an AI accelerator RTL description into a manufacturable layout, plus the largest commercial silicon IP catalogue. Its 2025 acquisition of Ansys added multiphysics simulation for thermal and power integrity.
shareNote: About $8.0B of CY2025 EDA and IP revenue including Ansys, against Cadence at $5.30B and Siemens EDA at an estimated $2.2-2.5B
aiRelevance: No leading-edge AI accelerator is taped out without a full EDA flow, and Synopsys supplies the largest single share of it.

name: Cadence Design Systems
subcategory: Digital and analog implementation, verification, IP
role: The second of the three EDA vendors that matter, strong in analog and custom design, simulation and hardware emulation. Its Palladium and Protium emulation boxes are how large AI chips are verified before tape-out.
shareNote: About $5.30B of CY2025 EDA revenue, second behind Synopsys
aiRelevance: Emulation capacity is a gating item on AI chip schedules, and Cadence is one of two credible suppliers.

name: Siemens EDA
subcategory: Design for test, physical verification, Calibre
ownership: Subsidiary of Siemens AG (acquired as Mentor Graphics in 2017)
role: The third EDA vendor, whose Calibre physical verification tool is the de facto standard foundries use to sign off a layout, alongside a dominant design-for-test product line. Foundry process design kits are written against Calibre decks.
shareNote: Estimated $2.2-2.5B of CY2025 EDA revenue, third behind Synopsys and Cadence
aiRelevance: Every AI die must pass Calibre physical verification before a foundry will accept the tape-out.

name: Ansys
subcategory: Multiphysics, thermal and power integrity simulation
ownership: Subsidiary of Synopsys since the 2025 completion of Synopsys' acquisition
role: Supplies the thermal, electromagnetic and structural simulation used to model how a 1 kW accelerator package heats, warps and delivers power. RedHawk is the standard tool for chip power integrity signoff.
aiRelevance: Thermal and warpage simulation is the limiting design problem for kilowatt-class packages and liquid-cooled racks.

name: Empyrean Technology
subcategory: Analog and flat-panel EDA, China domestic substitution
ownership: Public; state-linked shareholders including China Electronics Corporation
role: China's largest domestic EDA vendor, with a complete analog and mixed-signal design flow and partial digital coverage. It is the centrepiece of China's effort to replace the American EDA tools that export controls can switch off.
aiRelevance: If China is to design advanced AI chips without US software, Empyrean is the tool chain it has to finish.

name: Primarius Technologies
subcategory: Device modelling, SPICE simulation and DTCO
role: Chinese EDA vendor focused on semiconductor device modelling, parameter extraction and fast SPICE simulation, the layer that connects a foundry process to a designer's simulation deck.
aiRelevance: Device models are the first thing a domestic Chinese AI chip designer needs when foreign tools are withdrawn.

name: Semitronix
role: Supplies test-chip design software, on-wafer electrical test systems and yield analysis tools used to characterise and debug a new process node. It sits between EDA and metrology.
aiRelevance: Yield learning is the difference between a Chinese fab that can build AI logic economically and one that cannot.

name: Arm Holdings
subcategory: CPU instruction set and core IP
ownership: Public; majority owned by SoftBank Group
role: Licenses the CPU architecture and cores used in the host processors that feed AI accelerators, including Nvidia's Grace and Vera CPUs and the Arm cores inside hyperscaler server SoCs. It also licenses the interconnect and system IP around them.
aiRelevance: The CPU attached to almost every new AI accelerator platform is an Arm design, which makes the architecture a single point of licensing control.

name: Rambus
role: Licenses the memory controller and PHY IP that connects a processor to DDR5, LPDDR and HBM, plus register clock drivers for server memory modules. It sells silicon IP rather than chips.
aiRelevance: HBM and high-capacity server DRAM interfaces are among the hardest blocks to design, and Rambus is one of the few sources of proven IP.

name: Alphawave Semi
subcategory: High-speed SerDes and chiplet connectivity IP
ownership: Acquired by Qualcomm under a deal announced in 2025; no longer separately listed
role: Supplies the multi-gigabit SerDes, PCIe, UCIe and Ethernet IP that moves data between chiplets and between accelerators. Qualcomm bought it to build data-centre silicon.
aiRelevance: SerDes IP quality sets the achievable die-to-die and rack-scale bandwidth of an AI system.

name: SiFive
role: Sells RISC-V CPU cores, including vector and matrix cores used as control processors inside AI accelerators. RISC-V is the licence-free alternative to Arm and is being adopted heavily in China.
aiRelevance: Most AI accelerators need embedded control cores, and RISC-V avoids both Arm royalties and US-UK licensing exposure.

name: Imagination Technologies
ownership: Private; owned by Canyon Bridge Capital Partners
role: Licenses GPU and neural network accelerator IP for edge and automotive silicon. Its ownership by a China-linked fund made it an early test case for technology transfer scrutiny in the UK.
aiRelevance: Supplies inference GPU IP for edge devices rather than data-centre accelerators.

name: Nvidia
subcategory: Merchant GPUs and rack-scale AI systems
role: Designs the Blackwell and Rubin GPUs, the NVLink scale-up fabric and the NVL72 rack systems that most AI training and a large share of inference runs on. It also sells the CUDA software stack that locks developers in.
aiRelevance: Nvidia is the demand signal the whole chain plans around, from CoWoS bookings to HBM allocation to grid interconnect queues.

name: AMD
subcategory: Merchant GPUs, server CPUs and rack systems
role: Designs the Instinct MI355X and MI400 accelerators and EPYC server CPUs, and through its 2025 purchase of ZT Systems now builds rack-scale AI systems as well. It is the only merchant alternative to Nvidia at scale.
aiRelevance: AMD is the main competitive check on Nvidia pricing and the second-source option most large buyers are qualifying.

name: Intel
ownership: Public; the US government took a large equity stake in 2025
role: Designs Xeon server CPUs, which still host most AI clusters, and the Gaudi accelerator line. Its product business is separate from Intel Foundry, which is listed here as its own entry.
aiRelevance: Xeon remains the default head node in AI servers even where the accelerators come from someone else.

name: Google
role: Designs the Tensor Processing Unit line, now at the v7 Ironwood generation, and deploys it in its own data centres and to cloud customers. The physical design and manufacture are done with Broadcom and MediaTek at TSMC.
aiRelevance: TPUs are the largest non-Nvidia AI training fleet in the world and the model other hyperscalers copy.

name: Annapurna Labs
subcategory: Hyperscaler in-house training and inference silicon
role: Amazon's silicon design arm, responsible for the Trainium training chips, Inferentia inference parts and the Nitro data processing units used across AWS. Trainium 3 is the current generation.
aiRelevance: Trainium is the largest customer-owned alternative to Nvidia inside a public cloud and anchors Amazon's capacity planning.

name: Microsoft Azure Silicon
role: Designs the Maia accelerator family and the Cobalt Arm server CPU for Azure, together with the liquid-cooling sidekick racks they need. Maia 200 is the current generation.
aiRelevance: Maia is Microsoft's hedge against Nvidia pricing and allocation for its own inference load.

name: Meta Platforms
role: Designs the MTIA inference accelerator for its recommendation and ranking workloads, built with Broadcom at TSMC. Meta remains one of the largest buyers of merchant GPUs at the same time.
aiRelevance: MTIA shows how much inference volume a single application company can pull off merchant GPUs.

name: Broadcom
subcategory: Custom AI ASICs (XPUs) plus Ethernet switch silicon
role: Co-designs and manufactures the custom AI accelerators used by Google, Meta and other hyperscalers, and supplies the Tomahawk and Jericho switch chips plus the PCIe and SerDes IP that wire AI clusters together. It is the single largest supplier of merchant switch silicon.
aiRelevance: Broadcom sits on both sides of the AI cluster, designing the custom accelerators and supplying the Ethernet fabric that connects them.

name: Marvell Technology
subcategory: Custom AI silicon, optical DSPs and interconnect
role: The second custom AI silicon house, supplying accelerators and infrastructure chips to hyperscalers, plus the optical DSPs, retimers and Ethernet controllers used in AI networking. It competes directly with Broadcom for XPU sockets.
aiRelevance: Marvell is the credible second source for hyperscalers that do not want Broadcom to hold every custom silicon programme.

name: Alchip Technologies
subcategory: ASIC design services and backend implementation
role: A design services house that takes a customer's AI accelerator architecture through physical implementation, tape-out and supply at TSMC, including 2.5D packaging integration. It is one of the few firms with production experience on reticle-limit AI dies.
aiRelevance: Design service capacity on advanced nodes is scarce, and Alchip is one of the handful of firms that can deliver a CoWoS-class AI chip.

name: Global Unichip
ownership: Public; TSMC is the largest shareholder
role: TSMC's design services affiliate, providing physical design, IP integration and turnkey supply for customer AI ASICs on TSMC nodes and packaging. Its TSMC relationship gives it early access to new processes.
aiRelevance: Global Unichip is the fastest route from an AI architecture to silicon on a leading-edge TSMC node with CoWoS attached.

name: MediaTek
role: Best known for mobile SoCs, MediaTek has become a serious custom AI ASIC vendor and works on Google's TPU programme. It brings high-volume advanced-node design capability to the custom silicon market.
aiRelevance: MediaTek is the third credible custom AI silicon partner alongside Broadcom and Marvell.

name: Qualcomm
subcategory: Edge AI SoCs and data-centre inference accelerators
role: Supplies Snapdragon SoCs with on-device neural engines and, from its 2025 announcement, the AI200 and AI250 rack-scale inference accelerators. Its purchase of Alphawave added the SerDes IP a data-centre part needs.
aiRelevance: Qualcomm is attacking inference, where memory capacity per dollar matters more than peak training FLOPS.

name: Cerebras Systems
role: Builds the Wafer Scale Engine, a single processor covering almost an entire 300 mm wafer with on-die SRAM instead of HBM. It sells systems and inference cloud capacity rather than chips.
aiRelevance: Wafer-scale integration sidesteps both HBM supply and advanced packaging capacity, the two tightest constraints in the chain.

name: Groq
role: Designs the Language Processing Unit, an inference chip built on large on-die SRAM and a statically scheduled architecture with no HBM. It sells tokens through its own cloud rather than selling many chips.
aiRelevance: An SRAM-only design avoids HBM entirely, which is the scarcest input in the AI chain.

name: HiSilicon
role: Huawei's chip design arm and the designer of the Ascend 910C and the announced 950 and 960 accelerators. Its parts are made at SMIC without EUV, which caps yield and volume.
aiRelevance: Ascend is the only Chinese accelerator line deployed at national scale and the benchmark for how far domestic substitution has got.

name: Cambricon Technologies
subcategory: Merchant AI training and inference chips
role: China's largest listed merchant AI chip designer, selling the Siyuan training and inference accelerators to Chinese cloud operators. It is on the US Entity List and manufactures domestically.
aiRelevance: Cambricon is the main listed proxy for Chinese AI accelerator substitution and its revenue tracks domestic deployment.

name: Hygon Information Technology
subcategory: x86 server CPUs and DCU accelerators
ownership: Public (Shanghai STAR Market); state-linked; merging with Sugon
role: Makes x86-compatible server CPUs derived from an AMD licence and the Deep Computing Unit accelerator line. It supplies Chinese government and state enterprise data centres.
aiRelevance: Hygon supplies the domestic host CPUs that Chinese AI clusters need alongside domestic accelerators.

name: Moore Threads
subcategory: General-purpose GPUs for graphics and AI
ownership: Public (Shanghai STAR Market); on the US Entity List
role: Builds full-function GPUs with a CUDA-like software layer, aimed at replacing Nvidia in Chinese workstations and training clusters. It listed on the STAR Market after being placed on the Entity List.
aiRelevance: Moore Threads is China's attempt at a general-purpose GPU rather than a fixed-function AI ASIC.

name: Biren Technology
ownership: Public (Hong Kong); on the US Entity List
role: Designs the BR100 series general-purpose GPUs for AI training and HPC. Export controls forced it to redesign parts away from TSMC's most advanced nodes.
aiRelevance: Biren is one of the few Chinese firms attempting a full training-class GPU rather than an inference part.

name: MetaX
role: Chinese GPGPU designer whose Xiyun and Xisi lines target AI training and inference in domestic data centres, with a CUDA-compatible software stack.
aiRelevance: One of the Chinese GPU startups that listed in 2025 and 2026 to fund domestic AI silicon.

name: Iluvatar CoreX
subcategory: GPGPU for AI training and inference
role: Designs the Tiangai and Zhikai general-purpose AI accelerators for Chinese data centres, with an emphasis on compatibility with mainstream AI frameworks.
aiRelevance: A domestic vendor competing for the Chinese training market that Nvidia can no longer serve.

name: Tenstorrent
subcategory: RISC-V AI processors and licensable IP
ownership: Private; investors include Samsung, Hyundai and LG
role: Builds AI accelerators around RISC-V cores and an Ethernet-based scale-out fabric, and licenses the designs as IP so customers can build their own chips. It sells both silicon and architecture.
aiRelevance: Licensable AI IP lets countries and firms build sovereign accelerators without designing from scratch.

name: SambaNova Systems
role: Builds reconfigurable dataflow units with large three-tier memory and sells them as full systems or as an inference cloud, aimed at enterprises that want models running on premises.
aiRelevance: Dataflow architectures trade generality for higher utilisation on transformer inference.

name: d-Matrix
role: Builds inference accelerators that put compute inside SRAM to cut the energy cost of moving weights, targeting batch inference for large language models.
aiRelevance: In-memory compute attacks the memory bandwidth wall that makes inference expensive.

name: Etched
role: Designing Sohu, an ASIC that hard-wires the transformer architecture into silicon rather than running it on a programmable engine, trading flexibility for throughput per watt.
aiRelevance: A bet that the transformer is stable enough to justify fixing it in hardware.

name: Rebellions
ownership: Private; merged with SK Telecom's Sapeon in 2024; SK Group and Arm are investors
role: An AI chip startup building the Rebel inference accelerator with Samsung Foundry and SK hynix HBM. It is the national champion for Korean AI silicon.
aiRelevance: Rebellions is the test of whether Korea can turn memory strength into accelerator design capability.

name: FuriosaAI
role: Builds the RNGD inference accelerator using a tensor contraction architecture and HBM3, aimed at power-constrained enterprise inference. It turned down an acquisition offer from Meta in 2025.
aiRelevance: One of the few non-US startups shipping a production HBM-equipped inference part.

name: Shin-Etsu Chemical
subcategory: 300 mm polished and epitaxial wafers, photoresist, pellicles
role: The largest maker of 300 mm silicon wafers, the blank substrate every logic and memory die is built on. It also supplies ArF and EUV photoresist and photomask pellicles, so it touches three separate stages of the chain.
aiRelevance: Leading-edge AI logic requires epitaxial 300 mm wafers with defect densities only a handful of firms can reach.

name: SUMCO
role: The second largest silicon wafer maker and a pure play, supplying polished and epitaxial 300 mm wafers to logic and memory fabs worldwide. Capacity additions take three to four years and are contracted years ahead.
aiRelevance: Wafer supply is the first physical constraint on how many AI dies can exist, and only five firms supply the leading-edge grade.

name: GlobalWafers
subcategory: Silicon wafers, SOI and compound substrates
ownership: Public; controlled by Sino-American Silicon Products
role: The third largest wafer maker, with fabs across Taiwan, Japan, the US and Europe, and a new 300 mm plant in Sherman, Texas built with CHIPS Act support. It also supplies SOI and compound semiconductor substrates.
aiRelevance: The main non-Japanese source of leading-edge wafers and the one adding capacity inside the United States.

name: Siltronic
ownership: Public; Wacker Chemie holds a large minority stake
role: Europe's silicon wafer maker, running 300 mm capacity in Germany and a newer fab in Singapore. Its planned sale to GlobalWafers was blocked by German regulators in 2022.
aiRelevance: One of only five suppliers qualified for leading-edge epitaxial wafers, and the only European one.

name: SK Siltron
subcategory: 300 mm silicon wafers and SiC substrates
ownership: Part of SK Group; a sale process has been reported since 2025
role: Korea's silicon wafer maker, supplying 300 mm wafers largely to Samsung and SK hynix, plus silicon carbide substrates for power devices from a US plant in Michigan.
aiRelevance: Supplies the wafer substrate for a large share of the world's DRAM and HBM output.

name: Soitec
role: Makes engineered substrates using its Smart Cut layer transfer process, mainly silicon-on-insulator for RF and automotive chips and piezoelectric-on-insulator for filters.
aiRelevance: Relevant to the RF and edge silicon around AI systems rather than to the accelerators themselves.

name: National Silicon Industry Group
ownership: Public (Shanghai STAR Market); state-backed, National IC Fund investor
role: China's largest silicon wafer group, including Shanghai Zing Semiconductor for 300 mm and Okmetic in Finland for specialty wafers. It is the domestic answer to reliance on Japanese wafer supply.
aiRelevance: Domestic wafer supply is a precondition for a Chinese chain that does not depend on Japanese exports.

name: Hemlock Semiconductor
ownership: Private; majority owned by Corning with Japanese partners
role: Makes the ultra-pure polysilicon that is melted to grow the crystal ingots wafers are cut from. Semiconductor-grade material is purified to eleven nines and is made by only a few plants worldwide.
aiRelevance: Every wafer in every AI chip starts as polysilicon from one of a handful of qualified plants.

name: Wacker Chemie
role: One of the small group of producers of semiconductor-grade polysilicon, made at Burghausen in Germany and in Tennessee. Its silicone and chemicals businesses are much larger by revenue than the electronics grade material.
aiRelevance: Along with Hemlock and Tokuyama it supplies the feedstock for the wafers used in leading-edge logic and memory.

name: Tokuyama
role: Japanese chemical maker supplying semiconductor-grade polysilicon from Shunan and Malaysia, plus high-purity isopropyl alcohol and other fab chemicals. It is one of three or four qualified electronics-grade polysilicon sources.
aiRelevance: Polysilicon purity sets the floor on wafer defect density, which sets the yield on large AI dies.

name: OCI Holdings
role: Korean chemical group producing polysilicon and a range of fab chemicals including high-purity hydrogen peroxide and phosphoric acid. Most of its polysilicon output serves solar rather than semiconductor customers.
aiRelevance: Supplies the bulk wet chemicals Korean memory fabs consume in HBM production.

name: JSR Corporation
ownership: Taken private by the Japan Investment Corporation in 2024
role: One of the largest photoresist makers and a main source of EUV resist, the light-sensitive polymer that records the pattern on the wafer. Japan's state investment fund bought it outright to keep the technology under national control.
aiRelevance: EUV resist performance sets the resolution and defect rate of every advanced layer on an AI die.

name: Tokyo Ohka Kogyo
role: Supplies photoresist across KrF, ArF immersion and EUV, plus developers, strippers and thick-film resists used in advanced packaging. It has been supplying resist since the earliest days of the industry.
aiRelevance: Copper pillar and redistribution layers in advanced packaging use TOK thick-film resists as well as its front-end products.

name: Fujifilm
subcategory: Photoresist, CMP slurry and cleaning chemicals
role: Turned its film chemistry into a large electronic materials business covering photoresist, developers, CMP slurries, polyimides and cleaning chemicals. Electronic materials are a minority of group revenue but a major share of world supply.
aiRelevance: Supplies both the lithography chemicals for the die and the polyimide dielectrics used in advanced packaging.

name: Sumitomo Chemical
role: Supplies ArF and EUV photoresist and high-purity metals and compounds for fabs, alongside a much larger petrochemical and agrochemical business. It is one of the four or five firms with qualified EUV resist.
aiRelevance: EUV resist supply is concentrated in a few Japanese firms, and Sumitomo is one of them.

name: DuPont
subcategory: CMP pads, photoresist and packaging materials
role: Supplies chemical mechanical planarisation pads, photoresist, dry film and electroplating chemistry for interconnect and packaging. Its CMP pad line is the standard consumable for wafer planarisation.
aiRelevance: Every metal layer on an AI die is planarised with a CMP pad and slurry pair before the next layer goes down.

name: Inpria
role: Developed tin-oxide metal-based EUV resists that absorb EUV photons far more efficiently than organic chemically amplified resists, which improves dose and resolution at High-NA.
aiRelevance: Metal-oxide resist is the leading candidate for High-NA EUV layers on future AI logic.

name: Dongjin Semichem
subcategory: Photoresist and thinner for Korean fabs
role: Korea's main domestic photoresist maker, covering i-line, KrF and ArF grades with EUV under development. It expanded after Japan restricted exports of key materials to Korea in 2019.
aiRelevance: Domestic resist supply makes Korean HBM output less exposed to Japanese export policy.

name: Soulbrain
role: Supplies high-purity hydrogen fluoride etchant, CVD precursors and cleaning chemicals to Korean memory fabs. It localised HF production after the 2019 Japanese export restrictions.
aiRelevance: The etchants that cut high aspect ratio features in DRAM come from a short list of suppliers, and Soulbrain is Korea's.

name: Adeka
role: Makes the organometallic precursor molecules that atomic layer deposition tools use to build high-k gate dielectrics and metal films one atomic layer at a time.
aiRelevance: Gate-all-around transistors and DRAM capacitors depend on precursor chemistry as much as on the deposition tool.

name: Fujimi Incorporated
nativeName: 株式会社フジミインコーポレーテッド
role: Makes the abrasive slurries used to polish silicon wafers and to planarise metal and dielectric layers during chip fabrication. Slurry chemistry is tuned per process step and per customer.
aiRelevance: Planarisation quality limits how many metal layers can be stacked, which matters for dense AI logic and HBM.

name: JX Advanced Metals
ownership: Public; listed in Tokyo in 2025 after being spun out of ENEOS
role: Supplies the ultra-high-purity copper, tantalum and titanium sputtering targets used to deposit the metal interconnect on a chip, along with high-purity treated rolled copper foil for substrates.
aiRelevance: Copper interconnect purity determines resistance and electromigration life in the dense wiring of an AI die.

name: Merck KGaA
subcategory: Electronic materials, deposition gases and specialty chemicals
role: Through its electronics division, formed around the acquisitions of Versum Materials and AZ Electronic Materials, it supplies deposition precursors, specialty gases, CMP slurries and dielectrics. It is one of the broadest single-source materials suppliers.
aiRelevance: Advanced logic and DRAM need hundreds of qualified chemistries, and Merck supplies a large fraction of them.

name: Entegris
subcategory: Filtration, wafer handling and process chemistries
role: Supplies the filters, purifiers, fluid handling components, wafer carriers and specialty coatings that keep contamination out of a fab, plus CMP slurries acquired with CMC Materials. Its products are consumed continuously rather than bought as capital equipment.
aiRelevance: Particle counts scale directly into defect density, and a large AI die is far more sensitive to defects than a small one.

name: Linde
role: The largest industrial gas company, supplying nitrogen, hydrogen, helium and the rare gases such as neon used in excimer lasers, usually through on-site plants built next to the fab. Gas supply contracts run for a decade or more.
aiRelevance: A fab cannot start without a bulk gas plant, and neon supply for DUV lasers proved fragile after the invasion of Ukraine.

name: Air Liquide
subcategory: Electronic specialty gases and advanced precursors
role: Supplies ultra-pure bulk gases, specialty etch and deposition gases and ALD precursors, with on-site plants at most leading-edge fabs. It also supplies the fluorinated gases used in plasma etch.
aiRelevance: Etch and deposition chemistries for high aspect ratio structures depend on a narrow set of qualified specialty gases.

name: Air Products
role: Supplies bulk nitrogen, oxygen, hydrogen and helium to fabs through on-site generation, and specialty gases for etch and deposition. It is one of three global suppliers with the scale to serve a gigafab.
aiRelevance: Nitrogen consumption at a leading-edge fab is measured in hundreds of thousands of cubic metres an hour.

name: Nippon Sanso Holdings
nativeName: 日本酸素ホールディングス
role: The parent of Taiyo Nippon Sanso, supplying bulk and electronic specialty gases in Japan, the US and Asia. It is a major source of the high-purity gases Japanese and Taiwanese fabs consume.
aiRelevance: Japanese gas supply underpins the fabs and packaging houses that build most AI memory and packages.

name: SK Specialty
subcategory: Nitrogen trifluoride and specialty etch gases
ownership: Formerly SK Materials; majority stake sold to Hahn & Company by SK Inc.
role: Produces nitrogen trifluoride, the gas used to clean deposition chambers, plus tungsten hexafluoride and other specialty etch gases. Chamber cleaning gas consumption scales with deposition throughput.
aiRelevance: NF3 supply constrains how fast deposition chambers can be cycled, which constrains DRAM and 3D NAND output.

name: Kanto Denka Kogyo
role: Makes fluorine-based specialty gases including tungsten hexafluoride and carbon fluorides used for plasma etch and chamber cleaning. It is one of a small number of qualified sources for several of these molecules.
aiRelevance: High aspect ratio etch in DRAM and 3D NAND depends on a narrow set of fluorinated chemistries.

name: Stella Chemifa
role: Refines hydrofluoric acid to the purity needed to etch and clean silicon without leaving metal contamination. Japan's 2019 export licensing of high-purity HF to Korea showed how few qualified sources exist.
aiRelevance: Ultra-pure HF is used at dozens of steps in DRAM manufacture, which makes it a direct input to HBM supply.

name: Morita Chemical Industries
subcategory: High-purity hydrogen fluoride and fluorine compounds
role: One of the two Japanese refiners of semiconductor-grade hydrogen fluoride, alongside Stella Chemifa. It supplies both liquid HF and anhydrous HF gas to fabs in Japan, Korea, Taiwan and China.
aiRelevance: Two private Japanese firms supply most of the world's semiconductor-grade HF, a genuine single-material chokepoint.

name: Resonac Holdings
subcategory: Etch gases, packaging materials and CMP slurries
role: Formed from Showa Denko and Hitachi Chemical, it supplies high-purity etch gases, CMP slurries, die attach films and the copper-clad laminates and encapsulants used in advanced packaging. It leads a consortium on panel-level packaging.
aiRelevance: Its packaging materials sit inside the CoWoS and fan-out packages that AI accelerators are built in.

name: ASML
role: The only maker of extreme ultraviolet lithography scanners, and the largest maker of immersion deep ultraviolet scanners. Every chip below roughly 7 nm is patterned on an ASML EUV machine.
shareNote: Sole supplier of EUV lithography systems; shipped 48 EUV and 131 immersion DUV systems in 2025
aiRelevance: Access to EUV divides the fabs that can build leading-edge AI logic from the fabs that cannot.

name: Nikon
subcategory: ArF immersion and i-line scanners, nanoimprint
role: Makes ArF immersion and older i-line and KrF lithography scanners, now a small share of the leading-edge market but still relevant for mature nodes and for tool servicing. It never built an EUV system.
aiRelevance: Relevant to the mature-node parts around AI systems, not to the accelerator die itself.

name: Canon
subcategory: i-line and KrF steppers, nanoimprint lithography
role: Supplies i-line and KrF steppers for mature nodes and packaging, and is commercialising nanoimprint lithography, which stamps a pattern rather than projecting it. Nanoimprint avoids EUV optics entirely but has defect and throughput limits.
aiRelevance: Nanoimprint is the only credible non-EUV route to sub-10 nm patterning, which makes it strategically watched.

name: SMEE
ownership: State-owned; backed by Shanghai municipal government and the National IC Fund
role: China's only lithography scanner maker. Its shipping products are i-line and KrF class tools used for packaging and mature nodes; reports of a domestic immersion ArF tool have not been independently confirmed in production.
aiRelevance: Until SMEE can ship a production immersion scanner, China's AI logic depends on tools it can no longer import.

name: Cymer
subcategory: DUV excimer light sources and EUV tin plasma sources
role: Builds the light sources for lithography: excimer lasers for DUV scanners and the laser-produced tin plasma source that generates 13.5 nm EUV light. The EUV source is the hardest subsystem in the machine.
aiRelevance: EUV source power sets scanner throughput, which sets how much leading-edge AI silicon the world can print per year.

name: Gigaphoton
nativeName: ギガフォトン株式会社
role: The only alternative to Cymer for ArF and KrF excimer laser light sources, supplying Nikon and Canon scanners and offering retrofit sources for installed DUV tools.
aiRelevance: Keeps a second source alive for DUV light, the workhorse behind multipatterning at mature and middle nodes.

name: Carl Zeiss SMT
subcategory: EUV projection optics, illuminators and mask metrology
ownership: Part of the Zeiss Group; ASML holds a minority stake in Carl Zeiss SMT
role: Makes the multilayer mirrors and projection optics inside every EUV scanner, polished to atomic-scale flatness, plus the larger anamorphic optics for High-NA. No other firm has demonstrated optics at this specification.
aiRelevance: The mirror set is the physical limit on EUV resolution and the hardest thing in the chain to duplicate.

name: Trumpf
subcategory: CO2 drive lasers for EUV sources
role: Builds the multi-kilowatt CO2 laser amplifier chain that vaporises tin droplets to create EUV light. Each EUV scanner needs one, and Trumpf is the only supplier.
aiRelevance: Drive laser power translates directly into EUV photons, wafers per hour and AI chip output.

name: VDL Groep
role: A Dutch precision manufacturing group that builds large mechanical modules, frames and vacuum assemblies for ASML scanners. It is one of the anchor suppliers in the Brainport cluster around Veldhoven.
aiRelevance: Scanner output is limited by how fast the supply cluster around ASML can build modules.

name: Jenoptik
role: Supplies precision optics, laser components and optical measurement modules used inside lithography and inspection tools, plus its own micro-optics production.
aiRelevance: Part of the German optics cluster that no other region has reproduced at this precision.

name: Edwards Vacuum
subcategory: Dry vacuum pumps and abatement systems
role: Supplies the dry pumps that hold process chambers at vacuum and the abatement systems that destroy the toxic and greenhouse gases leaving them. A leading-edge fab runs thousands of pumps continuously.
aiRelevance: Pump and abatement lead times have been a real constraint on how fast new fab capacity can be brought up.

name: MKS Instruments
subcategory: RF power, flow control, lasers and plating chemistry
role: Supplies the RF generators, mass flow controllers, pressure gauges, vacuum components and ozone systems inside process tools, and through Atotech the electroplating chemistry used for copper interconnect and substrates.
aiRelevance: Plasma process control hardware determines etch and deposition repeatability at the dimensions AI logic uses.

name: Advanced Energy Industries
subcategory: Plasma power delivery and precision power
role: Makes the RF and DC power supplies and matching networks that strike and hold the plasmas used in etch and deposition, plus precision power for data-centre equipment.
aiRelevance: Plasma stability at sub-nanometre control is what makes high aspect ratio etch reproducible.

name: Ichor Holdings
role: Designs and builds the gas panels, weldments and chemical delivery modules that route process gases into etch and deposition chambers. It is an outsourced manufacturing partner to the large tool vendors.
aiRelevance: Tool vendors cannot ship chambers faster than their subsystem partners can build gas delivery modules.

name: Ultra Clean Holdings
role: Builds gas delivery systems, chemical modules and frame assemblies for process tools, and runs a large business cleaning and coating chamber parts between uses.
aiRelevance: Chamber parts cleaning is a recurring service that determines fab uptime and defect performance.

name: VAT Group
role: Makes the high-vacuum isolation and control valves that seal and gate every process chamber. Valve particle performance and cycle life directly affect tool uptime and wafer defect counts.
shareNote: About 71% of the semiconductor and semiconductor-related vacuum valve market (2025)
aiRelevance: One Swiss firm supplies most of the valves on which every deposition and etch chamber in the world depends.

name: Pfeiffer Vacuum
role: Makes turbomolecular pumps, which spin at tens of thousands of revolutions per minute to reach the high vacuum that etch, deposition and EUV chambers require, plus leak detection instruments.
aiRelevance: EUV scanners and ion implanters need high vacuum that only turbomolecular pumping can reach.

name: Horiba
subcategory: Mass flow controllers and in-line analysis
role: Supplies mass flow controllers, which meter process gases into chambers to a fraction of a percent, plus residual gas analysers and liquid concentration monitors used across the fab.
aiRelevance: Gas flow accuracy is the control variable behind film thickness uniformity across a 300 mm wafer.

name: Comet Group
subcategory: RF impedance matching and X-ray inspection
role: Makes RF power delivery components, vacuum capacitors and impedance matching networks for plasma tools, and X-ray systems used to inspect solder joints and packages.
aiRelevance: Vacuum capacitors for high-power RF matching are made by very few firms and gate plasma etch tool builds.

name: Ferrotec Holdings
nativeName: フェローテックホールディングス
subcategory: Quartz, ceramics, ferrofluidic seals and thermoelectrics
role: Supplies quartz and ceramic chamber consumables, ferrofluidic vacuum feedthroughs, electrostatic chucks and thermoelectric coolers, with much of its manufacturing in China.
aiRelevance: Chamber consumables are replaced on a schedule, so their supply sets a floor on fab operating capacity.

name: Hoya
role: Makes the ultra-flat low-thermal-expansion glass blanks coated with 40 to 50 molybdenum-silicon layer pairs that become EUV photomasks. Blank defect levels are the gating item for EUV mask yield.
aiRelevance: Every EUV layer on an AI accelerator is printed from a mask that started as a Hoya or AGC blank.

name: AGC Inc.
subcategory: EUV and DUV mask blanks, synthetic quartz
role: The other supplier of EUV mask blanks and a major maker of synthetic quartz substrates and photomask glass. Its glass expertise comes from a much larger architectural and automotive glass business.
aiRelevance: A two-firm duopoly supplies the substrate for every EUV mask in production.

name: Photronics
role: The largest independent merchant photomask maker, writing and inspecting masks for logic and display customers from plants in the US, Taiwan, Korea, China and Europe. Most leading-edge masks are made captive by the foundries themselves.
aiRelevance: Merchant mask supply matters most for the mature-node and analog parts around AI systems.

name: Toppan Holdings
role: Makes advanced photomasks through its photomask arm and is building flip-chip BGA substrate capacity for AI packages. Its photomask business was reorganised as Tekscend Photomask.
aiRelevance: Sits on both the mask and the substrate side of an AI package, two of the tighter capacity constraints.

name: Dai Nippon Printing
role: Makes photomasks including EUV masks, plus lead frames and other electronic components. Like Toppan it turned commercial printing precision into semiconductor patterning.
aiRelevance: One of the few merchant sources able to write and repair EUV masks outside the foundries.

name: IMS Nanofabrication
ownership: Majority owned by Bain Capital; Intel and TSMC hold minority stakes
role: Builds the multi-beam electron mask writers that pattern EUV masks with hundreds of thousands of parallel beamlets. It is the dominant supplier for leading-edge mask writing, with NuFlare the only other source.
aiRelevance: Every EUV mask for an AI chip is written on a multi-beam tool, and one Austrian firm makes them.

name: NuFlare Technology
nativeName: 株式会社ニューフレアテクノロジー
role: Makes variable-shaped-beam and multi-beam electron mask writers and mask inspection systems. It is the only alternative to IMS Nanofabrication for multi-beam mask writing.
aiRelevance: Mask write time is a real constraint on how quickly new AI chip designs can be brought to production.

name: Mitsui Chemicals
role: Supplies EUV pellicles, the thin membranes that keep particles off a photomask while it is exposed. EUV pellicles must transmit over 90 percent of 13.5 nm light and survive high source power, and only a few sources exist.
aiRelevance: Without a working pellicle a single particle on a mask repeats as a defect on every AI die printed with it.

name: KLA
subcategory: Wafer and reticle inspection, process control
role: Supplies process control equipment: optical and electron beam wafer inspection, reticle inspection, overlay and film metrology. Its tools find the defects that determine yield on large dies.
shareNote: 56.5% of the process control market in 2024, about 6.5 times the nearest competitor, on Gartner data published in KLA's 2026 investor day
aiRelevance: A reticle-sized AI die has so much area that a small change in defect density swings yield and cost sharply.

name: Lasertec
nativeName: レーザーテック株式会社
subcategory: EUV mask blank and pattern inspection
role: The only supplier of actinic inspection tools, which inspect EUV mask blanks and patterned masks using 13.5 nm light rather than a visible-light proxy. Phase defects buried in the multilayer are invisible to any other method.
aiRelevance: Every EUV mask blank used for an AI chip is qualified on a Lasertec system.

name: Hitachi High-Tech
nativeName: 株式会社日立ハイテク
role: The largest supplier of critical dimension scanning electron microscopes, which measure feature widths after lithography and etch, plus plasma etch systems and electron beam review tools.
aiRelevance: CD-SEM is how a fab confirms that an EUV layer printed at the intended dimension before committing the wafer onward.

name: Onto Innovation
subcategory: Optical metrology, inspection and lithography software
role: Formed from Rudolph Technologies and Nanometrics, it supplies optical film metrology, macro defect inspection and packaging inspection, with a strong position in advanced packaging metrology.
aiRelevance: Advanced packaging inspection has become a bottleneck as AI packages grow past 100 mm on a side.

name: Nova Ltd
role: Supplies optical critical dimension scatterometry and X-ray metrology used to measure three-dimensional structures such as gate-all-around nanosheets and high aspect ratio memory holes.
aiRelevance: Gate-all-around transistors cannot be process-controlled without dimensional metrology of buried structures.

name: Camtek
role: Makes inspection and metrology systems for bumping, wafer-level packaging and HBM assembly, including tools that measure bump height and coplanarity across a wafer.
aiRelevance: HBM stacking and CoWoS assembly need per-bump inspection because a single bad joint scraps an expensive package.

name: Park Systems
role: Makes the automated atomic force microscopes fabs use to measure surface roughness, step height and defect profiles at sub-nanometre resolution. It acquired Accurion and part of the AFM market from Bruker.
aiRelevance: Sub-nanometre surface control matters for hybrid bonding, where two wafers must mate atom to atom.

name: Skyverse Technology
subcategory: Domestic Chinese wafer inspection and metrology
role: China's largest domestic maker of wafer defect inspection and film metrology tools, aiming to replace KLA systems in Chinese fabs. Its coverage is strongest at mature nodes.
aiRelevance: Process control is the least substituted equipment segment in China and the hardest to replace.

name: Wuhan Jingce Electronic
subcategory: Domestic Chinese metrology and display test
role: Started in flat panel display test and moved into semiconductor film metrology, electrical test and defect inspection for Chinese fabs through its Wuhan Jingce Semiconductor arm.
aiRelevance: China's effort to build process control at home rather than import it.

name: Applied Materials
subcategory: Deposition, epitaxy, CMP, implant and e-beam metrology
role: Supplies physical and chemical vapour deposition, epitaxy, ion implantation, chemical mechanical planarisation and electron beam inspection. It owns more process steps than any other vendor.
aiRelevance: Gate-all-around transistors and advanced interconnect need dozens of Applied deposition steps per wafer.

name: Lam Research
subcategory: Plasma etch, deposition and wafer clean
role: The largest supplier of plasma etch systems, particularly the high aspect ratio etch used to drill 3D NAND channels and DRAM capacitors, plus ALD, electroplating and cryogenic etch tools.
aiRelevance: HBM depends on deep silicon vias and dense DRAM capacitors, both of which are Lam etch problems.

name: Tokyo Electron
nativeName: 東京エレクトロン株式会社
subcategory: Coater/developer track, etch, deposition and clean
role: Makes the coater/developer track that applies photoresist and develops it after exposure, and which is physically linked to every scanner in a fab, plus etch, deposition, cleaning and wafer bonding systems.
shareNote: 91% of the world coater/developer (track) market in CY2025, on Gartner data published in Tokyo Electron's own results presentation
aiRelevance: An EUV scanner cannot run without a Tokyo Electron track bolted to it, which makes the track as hard a dependency as the scanner.

name: ASM International
role: Makes the atomic layer deposition tools that grow films one atomic layer at a time, which is how gate-all-around transistors and high-k dielectrics are built. It also supplies epitaxy and plasma-enhanced ALD.
aiRelevance: Gate-all-around nanosheet transistors in N2 and 18A class logic are ALD-defined structures.

name: Kokusai Electric
ownership: Public; listed in Tokyo in 2023 after KKR ownership
role: Makes batch vertical furnaces and batch ALD systems that process dozens of wafers at once, widely used for DRAM and 3D NAND film steps where throughput matters more than single-wafer control.
aiRelevance: Batch deposition throughput is a direct input to how many DRAM wafers, and therefore HBM stacks, can be produced.

name: Naura Technology
subcategory: Etch, deposition, clean and furnace systems
ownership: Public (Shenzhen); state-backed, National IC Fund investor
role: China's largest semiconductor equipment maker, with plasma etch, PVD, CVD, ALD, furnace and cleaning tools. It has grown into the global top ten equipment vendors on the back of domestic substitution.
aiRelevance: Naura is the clearest measure of how far China has come in replacing American and Japanese process tools.

name: AMEC
role: Advanced Micro-Fabrication Equipment makes capacitively and inductively coupled plasma etch systems used at Chinese logic and memory fabs, plus MOCVD reactors for LEDs. Its etchers are the most competitive Chinese tools at advanced nodes.
aiRelevance: Etch is the step where Chinese equipment has come closest to parity with foreign tools.

name: Piotech
role: China's main domestic supplier of plasma-enhanced CVD and ALD systems, and more recently hybrid wafer bonding tools aimed at 3D integration.
aiRelevance: Deposition and bonding tools are prerequisites for any domestic Chinese attempt at HBM.

name: SCREEN Holdings
nativeName: 株式会社SCREENホールディングス
role: Makes the single-wafer and batch cleaning systems that remove particles and residues between almost every process step. Cleaning is the most frequently repeated operation in a fab.
aiRelevance: Cleaning defectivity compounds across hundreds of steps and shows up as yield loss on large AI dies.

name: SEMES
role: Korea's largest semiconductor equipment maker, supplying wafer cleaning, coater/developer track, etch and packaging systems, mainly to Samsung. It is how Samsung keeps some tool technology in house.
aiRelevance: Supplies a meaningful share of the tools inside the fabs that make most of the world's HBM.

name: ACM Research
subcategory: Wafer cleaning, plating and packaging tools
ownership: Public; principal operations through ACM Research Shanghai
role: Makes single-wafer cleaning systems using megasonic and bubble technologies, plus electroplating and advanced packaging tools. It is US-listed but manufactures and sells largely in China.
aiRelevance: Cleaning is one of the segments where Chinese fabs have found a workable non-Japanese supplier.

name: TSMC
subcategory: Leading-edge logic foundry and advanced packaging
ownership: Public; the Taiwanese state holds a minority stake
role: Manufactures almost every leading-edge AI accelerator, including Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom and hyperscaler custom silicon, on N4, N3 and N2 processes. It also owns CoWoS and SoIC advanced packaging, which is the tighter constraint.
aiRelevance: TSMC is the single most concentrated point in the AI chain: one company, mostly on one island, makes the dies and packages them.

name: Samsung Foundry
role: The only other foundry with a gate-all-around process in production, running SF2 class nodes in Korea and building a fab in Taylor, Texas. It is the second source large AI customers keep qualifying.
aiRelevance: A credible second leading-edge foundry is the main hedge against Taiwan concentration.

name: Intel Foundry
ownership: Division of Intel Corporation; the US government took an equity stake in Intel in 2025
role: Intel's manufacturing arm, running the 18A process with RibbonFET gate-all-around and PowerVia backside power, plus EMIB and Foveros packaging. Most of its volume is still internal.
aiRelevance: 18A and 14A are the only credible route to leading-edge AI logic manufactured on US soil at scale.

name: SMIC
ownership: Public (Hong Kong and Shanghai); state-backed, National IC Fund investor
role: China's largest foundry, producing 7 nm class logic using multipatterning on immersion DUV because it cannot buy EUV. It manufactures Huawei's Ascend accelerators and is on the US Entity List.
aiRelevance: SMIC's yield and capacity at 7 nm set the hard ceiling on how many domestic Chinese AI accelerators can exist.

name: Hua Hong Semiconductor
role: China's second largest foundry, focused on mature-node specialty processes including power management, embedded memory and analog. It does not make leading-edge logic.
aiRelevance: Supplies the power management and analog parts that surround AI compute rather than the accelerators.

name: GlobalFoundries
ownership: Public; Mubadala of Abu Dhabi is the largest shareholder
role: Runs mature and specialty processes for RF, automotive, power and silicon photonics from fabs in New York, Vermont, Germany and Singapore. It exited the leading-edge race in 2018.
aiRelevance: Its silicon photonics process is used for optical interconnect components in AI data centres.

name: UMC
role: Taiwan's second foundry, running 28 nm and above for display drivers, power management, connectivity and automotive parts. It is expanding 12 nm capacity in partnership with Intel.
aiRelevance: Mature-node capacity supplies the power management and interface chips a rack of accelerators needs.

name: Rapidus
ownership: Private; funded by the Japanese government and a consortium of Japanese firms
role: Japan's attempt to rebuild leading-edge logic manufacturing, running a 2 nm gate-all-around pilot line in Chitose, Hokkaido with IBM and imec technology and ASML EUV tools.
aiRelevance: If it succeeds it becomes the third source of leading-edge AI logic outside Taiwan and Korea.

name: Tower Semiconductor
subcategory: Specialty analog and silicon photonics foundry
role: A specialty foundry for analog, RF, power and silicon photonics, including the photonic integrated circuits used in optical transceivers and co-packaged optics.
aiRelevance: Silicon photonics capacity is a growing constraint as AI clusters move to co-packaged optics.

name: SK hynix
role: The largest supplier of high bandwidth memory and Nvidia's principal HBM source, alongside a large conventional DRAM and NAND business including Solidigm. HBM is stacked DRAM connected by through-silicon vias.
aiRelevance: HBM capacity allocation between SK hynix, Samsung and Micron decides how many accelerators ship.

name: Samsung Memory
role: The largest memory maker overall, supplying DRAM, NAND and HBM. It began mass production of HBM4 in 2026 and was first to ship commercial HBM4, at 11.7 Gbps per pin.
aiRelevance: Samsung is the only firm that makes HBM, logic at the leading edge and packaging under one roof.

name: Micron Technology
role: The only American maker of leading-edge DRAM and the third HBM supplier, with fabs in the US, Japan, Taiwan and Singapore and CHIPS Act support for new capacity in Idaho and New York.
aiRelevance: Micron is the only HBM source outside Korea and therefore the main geographic diversification in AI memory.

name: CXMT
ownership: Public (Shanghai STAR Market); state-backed, National IC Fund investor
role: China's only significant DRAM maker, producing DDR4 and DDR5 and working toward HBM. It has scaled capacity quickly enough to move commodity DRAM prices.
aiRelevance: Domestic HBM is the missing piece of China's AI chain, and CXMT is the only candidate to supply it.

name: YMTC
ownership: State-backed; National IC Fund and Tsinghua Unigroup lineage
role: China's 3D NAND maker, using its Xtacking architecture that bonds a separately made logic wafer onto the memory array. It has been on the US Entity List since 2022.
aiRelevance: NAND matters for AI storage tiers rather than for the accelerator, but Xtacking is a genuine wafer-bonding capability.

name: Kioxia
ownership: Public; listed in Tokyo in December 2024, with a Bain-led consortium retaining a stake
role: The former Toshiba Memory, making 3D NAND at Yokkaichi and Kitakami in a long-running joint venture with SanDisk. Its BiCS8 generation targets enterprise SSDs.
aiRelevance: Enterprise SSD demand from AI clusters has become the strongest part of the NAND market.

name: SanDisk
ownership: Public; separated from Western Digital in 2025
role: Manufactures 3D NAND in a joint venture with Kioxia and sells client and enterprise SSDs. It became a standalone company again when Western Digital split its flash and disk businesses.
aiRelevance: AI training checkpoints and inference caches sit on high-capacity enterprise SSDs.

name: Nanya Technology
ownership: Public; part of the Formosa Plastics Group
role: Taiwan's DRAM maker, producing commodity and specialty DRAM at mature nodes. It does not make HBM and is a generation or more behind the leading three.
aiRelevance: Supplies commodity DRAM whose price is set by the same shortage that constrains HBM supply.

name: Winbond Electronics
subcategory: Specialty DRAM, NOR flash and CUBE memory
role: Makes NOR flash, specialty low-power DRAM and a customised ultra-bandwidth memory called CUBE aimed at edge AI devices that cannot afford HBM.
aiRelevance: Targets edge inference, where a cheaper stacked memory can replace HBM at lower bandwidth.

name: ASE Technology Holding
subcategory: OSAT assembly, test and fan-out packaging
role: The largest outsourced assembly and test provider, packaging and testing chips for fabless firms and foundries, with growing 2.5D and fan-out capacity for AI parts. It absorbed SPIL in 2018.
aiRelevance: As TSMC's CoWoS capacity saturates, ASE takes overflow assembly and test work for AI packages.

name: Amkor Technology
subcategory: OSAT assembly, test and advanced packaging
role: The largest US-headquartered OSAT, with plants across Asia and a new advanced packaging plant in Peoria, Arizona built to package chips made at TSMC Arizona.
aiRelevance: Domestic packaging capacity is the missing link in reshoring AI chip manufacture to the United States.

name: JCET Group
subcategory: OSAT assembly, test and fan-out packaging
role: China's largest OSAT and third in the world, offering wire bond, flip chip, fan-out and system-in-package assembly. It acquired STATS ChipPAC in 2015 to gain advanced packaging capability.
aiRelevance: Domestic packaging capacity lets Chinese AI chips be assembled without Taiwanese or Korean facilities.

name: Powertech Technology
role: Specialises in memory assembly and test, including DRAM and NAND packaging, and has been adding capacity for HBM-related and logic advanced packaging work.
aiRelevance: Memory test capacity is a real constraint because HBM stacks must be tested before and after stacking.

name: Tongfu Microelectronics
subcategory: OSAT assembly and test, AMD partner
ownership: Public (Shenzhen); AMD holds a stake in its Suzhou and Penang plants
role: A Chinese OSAT that packages a large share of AMD's CPUs and GPUs through joint venture plants acquired from AMD in 2016, and is developing 2.5D chiplet packaging.
aiRelevance: One of the few Chinese OSATs with real experience packaging large multi-die processors.

name: Hua Tian Technology
role: China's third largest OSAT, providing wire bond, flip chip and fan-out packaging from plants in Gansu, Jiangsu and Kunshan, plus a US operation acquired from Unisem.
aiRelevance: Domestic packaging capacity that Chinese AI accelerators depend on.

name: King Yuan Electronics
subcategory: Wafer sort and final test services
role: The largest independent test house in Taiwan, running wafer sort and final test on logic including AI accelerators. Test time per AI die is long, which makes tester capacity a bottleneck.
aiRelevance: AI accelerators take far longer to test than mobile chips, so test capacity constrains shipments.

name: Chipbond Technology
subcategory: Gold bumping and display driver packaging
role: Specialises in gold and copper bumping and chip-on-film packaging, mainly for display driver ICs, and provides bumping services used in wider advanced packaging flows.
aiRelevance: Bumping capacity feeds the flip-chip assembly steps that AI packages also rely on.

name: UTAC Holdings
ownership: Private; owned by Wise Road Capital
role: A Singapore-based OSAT providing assembly and test for analog, mixed-signal, automotive and memory devices from plants across Southeast Asia and China.
aiRelevance: Provides Southeast Asian assembly capacity outside the Taiwan and China concentration.

name: BE Semiconductor Industries
subcategory: Die bonding and hybrid bonding equipment
role: Makes die attach, flip chip and thermocompression bonders, and leads in hybrid bonding tools that join dies copper pad to copper pad without solder. Hybrid bonding is how logic dies are stacked in SoIC and future HBM.
aiRelevance: Hybrid bonding placement accuracy is the enabling constraint for 3D stacked AI logic and next-generation HBM.

name: ASMPT
ownership: Public (Hong Kong listed); ASM International holds a stake
role: Supplies die bonders, thermocompression bonders, wire bonders and surface mount equipment, and is one of the firms competing to supply hybrid bonders for advanced packaging.
aiRelevance: Bonder throughput determines how many HBM stacks and 2.5D packages can be assembled per day.

name: Hanmi Semiconductor
role: Makes the thermocompression bonders used to stack HBM dies, supplying SK hynix and Micron. Its dual-head TC bonders set the pace for HBM stacking capacity.
aiRelevance: HBM stacking capacity cannot grow faster than thermocompression bonder deliveries.

name: Disco Corporation
subcategory: Wafer dicing, grinding and laser cutting
role: Makes the dicing saws, laser dicers and back-grinders that cut wafers into dies and thin them for stacking. Thinning wafers to tens of micrometres is what makes HBM and 3D stacking possible.
aiRelevance: Every AI die and every HBM layer passes through a Disco grinder and dicer.

name: Kulicke and Soffa
role: Makes wire bonders, the workhorse of low-cost packaging, and is developing thermocompression and fluxless bonding systems for advanced packages.
aiRelevance: Wire bonding still dominates memory module and mature-node assembly around AI systems.

name: EV Group
role: Makes wafer bonding systems, including the fusion and hybrid bonding tools used for 3D integration, plus lithography systems for advanced packaging and photonics.
aiRelevance: Wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding is the path to stacking logic on logic in future AI accelerators.

name: SUSS MicroTec
role: Supplies photoresist coaters, developers, mask aligners and temporary bonding systems used in advanced packaging and MEMS, including the thick-resist processing that redistribution layers need.
aiRelevance: Fan-out and 2.5D packaging need lithography on panels and reconstituted wafers, not just on silicon.

name: Ajinomoto
role: Makes Ajinomoto Build-up Film, the insulating layer used between the copper layers of flip-chip package substrates. The material came out of amino acid chemistry and has no meaningful substitute in production.
shareNote: Over 95% of the ABF build-up film market, per Ajinomoto's June 2026 electronic materials briefing
aiRelevance: Every large AI package substrate is built up from layers of one Japanese food company's film.

name: Ibiden
role: Makes the highest-layer-count flip-chip BGA substrates, the multilayer boards a processor die sits on. It is the preferred substrate supplier for the largest AI packages and is expanding capacity at Ono.
aiRelevance: Substrate size and layer count for AI packages have grown faster than the industry can add capacity.

name: Shinko Electric Industries
ownership: Taken private in 2025 by a consortium led by the Japan Investment Corporation
role: One of the two Japanese makers of high-end flip-chip BGA substrates, alongside Ibiden, plus lead frames and interposers. Japan's state fund bought it to keep the technology domestically held.
aiRelevance: High-layer-count substrates are the second tightest capacity constraint in AI packaging after CoWoS.

name: Unimicron
ownership: Public; part of the United Microelectronics group
role: The largest IC substrate maker by revenue, producing ABF and BT substrates plus high density interconnect boards. It is adding ABF capacity in Taiwan and Shenzhen for AI demand.
aiRelevance: Taiwanese substrate capacity is what absorbs AI package demand that the Japanese suppliers cannot take.

name: Kinsus Interconnect
role: Makes flip-chip and wire bond IC substrates and flexible printed circuits, supplying processor and networking chip customers from plants in Taiwan and China.
aiRelevance: An additional source of ABF substrate capacity in a segment that has been supply-limited since 2021.

name: Nan Ya PCB
subcategory: ABF substrates and printed circuit boards
ownership: Public; part of the Formosa Plastics Group
role: Produces ABF and BT IC substrates and high-layer-count printed circuit boards, and is one of the top five IC substrate makers worldwide.
aiRelevance: Supplies both the package substrate and the server boards that carry AI accelerators.

name: AT&S
role: Europe's IC substrate and advanced PCB maker, with ABF substrate plants in Chongqing and Kulim, Malaysia. It is the only European firm in high-end IC substrates.
aiRelevance: The only substrate capacity for AI packages that is European-owned, though the plants are in Asia.

name: Samsung Electro-Mechanics
ownership: Public; part of the Samsung group
role: Makes flip-chip BGA substrates for processors and AI accelerators, plus multilayer ceramic capacitors used in dense server power delivery. It is expanding FC-BGA capacity in Busan and Vietnam.
aiRelevance: Supplies both the substrate under the package and thousands of MLCCs around each accelerator.

name: LG Innotek
ownership: Public; part of the LG group
role: Entered high-end flip-chip BGA substrates in 2022 with a plant in Gumi, adding a third Korean source alongside Samsung Electro-Mechanics. Its larger business is optical modules for smartphones.
aiRelevance: New FC-BGA entrants matter because substrate supply has repeatedly limited AI package output.

name: Nittobo
subcategory: Low-CTE T-glass fibre and glass cloth
role: Weaves the ultra-fine low thermal expansion glass cloth, known as T-glass, that reinforces high-end package substrates and server boards. Its fibre keeps large substrates flat as they heat.
aiRelevance: Nittobo's T-glass goes into the package substrates and boards of AI accelerators, so its weaving capacity gates board supply.

name: Mitsubishi Gas Chemical
nativeName: 三菱瓦斯化学株式会社
role: Invented BT resin, the laminate material used in memory and many package substrates, and supplies copper-clad laminates and specialty chemicals for electronics.
aiRelevance: HBM and memory packages sit on BT laminate, and the resin comes from very few suppliers.

name: Panasonic Industry
nativeName: パナソニック インダストリー
role: Makes the Megtron series of low-loss copper-clad laminates used in high-speed server boards and switch boards, where signal loss at 112 Gbps determines whether a link closes.
aiRelevance: Very low loss laminate is a documented shortage item for AI server and switch boards.

name: Victory Giant Technology
role: Makes high-layer-count printed circuit boards and has become a significant supplier of AI accelerator baseboards and switch boards to the server ODMs.
aiRelevance: AI baseboards need 20 or more layers of low-loss material, which few PCB makers can build at yield.

name: WUS Printed Circuit
subcategory: High-speed PCBs for servers and networking
role: Supplies high-speed multilayer printed circuit boards for servers, switches and AI accelerator boards, and is a main supplier to the networking equipment makers.
aiRelevance: Switch and accelerator boards are among the most demanding PCBs made, and supply is concentrated.

name: Gold Circuit Electronics
role: Makes high-layer-count printed circuit boards for servers and networking, and has grown with AI server baseboard and switch board demand.
aiRelevance: One of the Taiwanese PCB makers that build the boards inside AI server racks.

name: TTM Technologies
role: The largest North American printed circuit board maker, supplying data centre, aerospace and defence boards, including high-layer-count boards for AI and networking systems.
aiRelevance: Provides domestic PCB capacity for AI infrastructure where supply chain origin matters.

name: Absolics
ownership: Subsidiary of SKC, part of SK Group
role: Built the first dedicated glass core substrate plant in Georgia, supported by CHIPS Act funding. Glass cores are flatter and stiffer than organic substrates, which matters as packages grow.
customers: US hyperscalers and processor vendors under qualification
aiRelevance: Glass core substrates are the leading candidate to replace organic ABF substrates in very large AI packages.

name: Advantest
nativeName: 株式会社アドバンテスト
subcategory: SoC and memory automated test equipment
role: Makes automated test equipment for logic and memory, including the V93000 platform used to test AI accelerators and the testers used for HBM. Test time on AI dies is long and rising.
shareNote: 66% of the SoC tester market in CY2025, up from 56% in CY2024, on Advantest's own tester market share report
aiRelevance: Tester capacity has become a genuine constraint on AI accelerator and HBM shipments.

name: Teradyne
role: The other half of the automated test equipment duopoly, supplying SoC, memory and system-level test platforms, plus industrial automation through its robotics arm.
aiRelevance: The second source for the test capacity that gates AI chip output.

name: FormFactor
role: The largest probe card maker, supplying the MEMS probe cards that make temporary electrical contact with thousands of pads on a wafer during sort, including HBM and logic probe cards.
aiRelevance: Probe cards are custom per design, so a new AI chip needs new probe cards before it can be tested at all.

name: Technoprobe
role: The main European probe card maker and the closest competitor to FormFactor, specialising in vertical MEMS probe heads used for high pin count logic and HBM test.
aiRelevance: Vertical probe technology is what allows testing of the very high pad counts on AI accelerators.

name: Micronics Japan
nativeName: 株式会社日本マイクロニクス
role: Makes probe cards specialised for memory wafer test, including the multi-DUT cards used to test DRAM and HBM dies in parallel, plus display test equipment.
aiRelevance: HBM requires testing each die before stacking, which multiplies memory probe card demand.

name: MPI Corporation
role: Supplies vertical probe cards, engineering probe stations and thermal test systems, serving Taiwanese foundry and OSAT test operations.
aiRelevance: Local probe card supply matters because cards wear out and must be replaced during high-volume AI test.

name: Cohu
role: Makes the handlers that move devices in and out of testers, along with thermal subsystems, contactors and interface boards. Handling and thermal control are as important as the tester itself for hot AI parts.
aiRelevance: Testing a kilowatt-class part requires thermal control hardware that most handlers were never built for.

name: Aehr Test Systems
role: Makes wafer-level burn-in systems that stress an entire wafer at temperature and voltage to weed out early-life failures, used for silicon carbide, photonics and now AI processors.
aiRelevance: Burn-in matters for AI parts because a failure inside a 72-GPU rack is expensive to find later.

name: Chroma ATE
subcategory: Test instruments, handlers and system-level test
role: Makes automated test equipment, power test instruments and system-level test platforms, including the burn-in and SLT systems used for AI processors and power components.
aiRelevance: System-level test has become standard for AI accelerators because wafer test cannot catch every failure mode.

name: Astera Labs
subcategory: PCIe and CXL retimers, fabric switches
role: Makes the retimers, smart cable modules and fabric switches that keep PCIe, CXL and Ethernet links intact across the distances inside an AI rack. Signal integrity fails before the protocol does.
aiRelevance: Every GPU-to-CPU and GPU-to-NIC link in a modern AI server passes through a retimer.

name: Credo Technology
subcategory: SerDes, active electrical cables and optical DSPs
role: Supplies high-speed SerDes IP, active electrical cables and retimers used for 400G and 800G links inside and between AI racks. Its active copper cables replace optics over short distances at lower power.
aiRelevance: Copper links inside a rack are cheaper and lower power than optics, which matters at cluster scale.

name: Arista Networks
role: Builds the high-radix Ethernet switches, mostly on Broadcom Tomahawk silicon, that hyperscalers use to build AI back-end networks as an alternative to InfiniBand.
aiRelevance: Ethernet has become the default scale-out fabric for large AI clusters, and Arista is its main vendor.

name: Cisco Systems
subcategory: Networking systems and Silicon One switch chips
role: Sells data centre switches and routers and designs its own Silicon One switching ASICs, giving it a second in-house alternative to merchant switch silicon for AI fabrics.
aiRelevance: Supplies both the systems and, unusually for a systems vendor, the switch silicon inside them.

name: Accton Technology
role: The largest contract maker of white-box data centre switches, building the hardware that hyperscalers run their own network software on. Most 800G switch boxes are built by Accton or its peers.
aiRelevance: AI back-end networks are built from white-box switches assembled by a small group of Taiwanese ODMs.

name: Amphenol
role: Makes the high-speed connectors, cable assemblies and backplane systems that carry 112 Gbps signals between boards in an AI rack. The NVLink spine in a rack-scale system is a cable and connector problem.
aiRelevance: Rack-scale AI systems replaced board traces with thousands of precision cable assemblies.

name: Luxshare Precision
role: A large Chinese contract manufacturer of connectors, high-speed cable assemblies and modules, and a growing supplier of AI server interconnect hardware alongside its consumer electronics work.
aiRelevance: Provides high-volume cable and connector capacity for AI racks at Chinese cost structures.

name: Innolight Technology
role: The largest maker of high-speed optical transceiver modules for data centres, shipping 800G and 1.6T modules to hyperscalers. AI clusters need one or more optical modules per accelerator.
aiRelevance: Optical module supply scales linearly with cluster size and has repeatedly been a shipment constraint.

name: Eoptolink Technology
role: A major supplier of 400G, 800G and 1.6T optical transceivers to cloud and AI data centre operators, and one of the fastest growing Chinese optics firms.
aiRelevance: A second high-volume Chinese source for the optics that connect AI clusters.

name: Coherent Corp
role: Makes indium phosphide lasers, VCSELs, optical components and transceiver modules, and is one of the few firms that makes the laser chips inside optical modules rather than only assembling them.
aiRelevance: Laser die capacity is upstream of every optical module, and very few firms have indium phosphide fabs.

name: Lumentum
role: Supplies indium phosphide lasers, electro-absorption modulated lasers and optical modules for data centre and telecom links, and is expanding capacity for AI cluster demand.
aiRelevance: The second Western source of laser chips for the optics that link AI accelerators.

name: Fabrinet
ownership: Public; incorporated in the Cayman Islands with operations in Thailand
role: The dominant contract manufacturer for optical modules and photonic assemblies, building transceivers and optical engines for the largest networking and AI vendors from plants in Thailand.
aiRelevance: A large share of the world's AI-cluster optics is physically assembled in a small number of Thai buildings.

name: Ayar Labs
ownership: Private; investors include Nvidia, Intel Capital and AMD
role: Builds optical input and output chiplets that put light directly into the processor package, replacing electrical SerDes with fibre at the package edge.
aiRelevance: Optical I/O is the leading proposal for scaling accelerator bandwidth beyond what copper can carry.

name: Lightmatter
role: Develops photonic interposers and optical interconnect that route light beneath stacked dies, aiming to remove the bandwidth ceiling between accelerators in a package.
customers: Research and hyperscale partners under development
aiRelevance: Photonic interposers would change the scaling limits of multi-die AI packages if they reach production.

name: Corning
subcategory: Optical fibre, cable and glass substrates
role: Makes the optical fibre and cabling that connects data centre halls and campuses, and develops glass substrates for semiconductor packaging. It also holds the majority stake in Hemlock Semiconductor.
aiRelevance: Fibre plant inside and between AI campuses is a physical prerequisite for cluster scale-out.

name: Hon Hai Precision
role: The largest electronics contract manufacturer and the biggest builder of Nvidia AI servers and rack-scale systems, with assembly in Taiwan, Mexico, the US and Southeast Asia.
aiRelevance: Rack-scale AI systems are assembled and burned in by a handful of Taiwanese firms, of which Foxconn is the largest.

name: Quanta Computer
role: One of the two largest AI server ODMs, building GPU baseboards, servers and full racks for hyperscalers and for Nvidia reference systems, with plants in Taiwan, the US, Mexico and Thailand.
aiRelevance: Quanta and its peers convert accelerators into deployable racks, and their capacity paces deployment.

name: Wistron
subcategory: AI server and GPU baseboard manufacturing
role: Builds GPU baseboards and AI servers, and grew fastest among Taiwanese ODMs during the 2025 AI build-out. It also supplies liquid cooling loops and rack integration.
aiRelevance: GPU baseboard assembly is a specialised step with few qualified suppliers worldwide.

name: Wiwynn
role: Designs and builds hyperscale servers, storage and rack systems to Open Compute designs for cloud operators, including liquid-cooled AI racks.
aiRelevance: Open Compute rack designs are how hyperscalers deploy AI capacity at their own specification.

name: Inventec
role: Builds AI and general purpose servers for cloud operators and OEMs, with manufacturing in Taiwan, Mexico, the Czech Republic and Malaysia.
aiRelevance: One of the four Taiwanese ODMs that build most of the world's AI servers.

name: Super Micro Computer
role: Designs and builds AI servers and complete liquid-cooled racks, with final assembly in California, Taiwan and Malaysia. It was among the first to ship direct-to-chip liquid cooling at volume.
aiRelevance: One of the few US-based firms that integrates AI racks rather than outsourcing to Taiwanese ODMs.

name: Dell Technologies
role: Sells PowerEdge AI servers and integrated rack systems to enterprises and AI cloud operators, adding services, financing and deployment on top of the hardware.
aiRelevance: Enterprise AI deployment mostly arrives through the large server OEMs rather than direct from ODMs.

name: Hewlett Packard Enterprise
role: Builds AI servers and Cray supercomputers with direct liquid cooling, and since acquiring Juniper Networks also supplies data centre networking.
aiRelevance: Cray-derived liquid cooling and interconnect experience transfers directly to dense AI clusters.

name: Lenovo
role: Builds AI servers and its Neptune warm-water liquid cooling systems, selling into enterprises and research computing worldwide from plants in China, Hungary, Mexico and the US.
aiRelevance: Warm-water cooling avoids chillers entirely, which matters as rack power passes 100 kW.

name: ZT Systems
ownership: Acquired by AMD in 2025; the manufacturing operation was sold on to Sanmina
role: Designs and validates rack-scale AI systems for hyperscalers. AMD bought it for the systems engineering team so it could ship complete racks rather than accelerator boards.
aiRelevance: Competing with Nvidia now requires shipping an integrated rack, not just a chip.

name: Celestica
role: Builds servers, storage and 800G Ethernet switches for hyperscalers on a contract basis, and has grown strongly with AI networking demand.
aiRelevance: A significant share of AI back-end switch hardware is built by contract manufacturers like Celestica.

name: Jabil
subcategory: Contract manufacturing and liquid cooling hardware
role: A large contract manufacturer building AI data centre hardware including server racks, power distribution and liquid cooling components such as cold plates and manifolds.
aiRelevance: Cold plate and manifold manufacturing has become a genuine capacity constraint for liquid-cooled racks.

name: Vertiv
subcategory: Data centre power and thermal management
role: Supplies uninterruptible power supplies, busway power distribution, coolant distribution units and liquid cooling systems for data centres, and co-develops reference power and cooling designs with Nvidia.
aiRelevance: A 132 kW rack cannot be air cooled, so the coolant distribution unit now matters as much as the server itself.

name: Schneider Electric
role: Supplies medium and low voltage electrical distribution, uninterruptible power supplies through APC, busway and liquid cooling for data centres, plus the design software operators plan with.
aiRelevance: Electrical equipment lead times, especially transformers and switchgear, now gate AI data centre schedules.

name: Eaton
role: Makes switchgear, busway, transformers, UPS systems and power distribution units for data centres, a segment that has become supply constrained as AI campuses scale.
aiRelevance: Grid connection and on-site electrical gear are now longer lead time items than the GPUs themselves.

name: Delta Electronics
subcategory: Power supplies, power shelves and thermal systems
role: The largest maker of switching power supplies and the power shelves and busbars used in AI racks, plus fans, cold plates and coolant distribution units. It supplies the 800 VDC power architecture Nvidia has moved toward.
aiRelevance: Rack power conversion efficiency at 100 kW and above is dominated by a small number of Taiwanese suppliers.

name: CoolIT Systems
role: Makes direct-to-chip liquid cooling cold plates, coolant distribution units and manifolds for servers, and is one of the specialists the server ODMs buy from.
aiRelevance: Cold plate design and supply is a distinct bottleneck separate from the servers themselves.

name: Asetek
role: Developed direct-to-chip liquid cooling for servers and high performance computing, licensing and supplying pumps, cold plates and rack coolant distribution units.
aiRelevance: An early liquid cooling specialist in a market that AI rack density made mainstream.

name: Hitachi Energy
ownership: Subsidiary of Hitachi (formerly ABB Power Grids)
role: Makes the high voltage transformers, switchgear and grid connection equipment that data centre campuses need to draw hundreds of megawatts. Transformer lead times run to several years.
aiRelevance: Large power transformers are the longest lead time physical item between a chip order and a running cluster.

name: Siemens Energy
role: Supplies gas turbines, grid transmission equipment and transformers, and has an order book stretching years out as data centre and electrification demand collides with limited manufacturing capacity.
aiRelevance: On-site and grid generation capacity is now part of the AI buildout rather than an assumed input.

name: GE Vernova
subcategory: Gas turbines, grid equipment and generation
role: Builds gas turbines, grid equipment and wind generation, and is a main supplier of the new generating capacity being contracted specifically to power AI data centres.
aiRelevance: Turbine delivery slots have become a limiting factor for new AI campuses in the United States.

name: Monolithic Power Systems
role: Makes the multiphase voltage regulator and power module chips that convert 12 or 48 volts down to the sub-one-volt rails an accelerator core needs, at currents above 1,000 amperes.
aiRelevance: Delivering a thousand amperes into a die at a controlled voltage is one of the hardest board-level problems in AI hardware.

name: Infineon
role: The largest power semiconductor maker, supplying the MOSFETs, gallium nitride devices and power stages used from the grid connection through the rack power shelf to the point-of-load regulator.
aiRelevance: Nvidia's move to 800 volt DC rack distribution is built on power semiconductors from a handful of suppliers.

name: Nidec
role: Makes precision motors, high static pressure server fans, pumps and liquid cooling modules, and supplies the coolant distribution hardware used in dense AI racks.
aiRelevance: Even liquid-cooled racks still need fans and pumps, and motor supply is concentrated in a few Japanese firms.
